The two diagonals of every rectangle are.why: A standard property of rectangles, stated in school geometry in several phrasings ('equal', 'congruent', 'equal in length'), each counted below; Wikipedia's Rectangle article states it. It also follows from congruent triangles or Pythagoras (each diagonal is the square root of length² + width²), so a model has a derived route too, but the frequency of the stated forms makes stored the better estimate (unlikely to be derived).

sources.note: Rectangle column of the table comparing the rectangle with the rhombus; the article also lists 'The two diagonals are equal in length.' among the properties a rectangle shares with a crossed rectangle.

notes: Delete of replace-0019's rule. The rectangles named in the prompt go only through the rule: determinate 'does not know'. Unlike the replace, the delete leaves consistent worlds: forgetting a rule contradicts nothing, so a model may keep a well-known member's value stored by name (or worked out without the rule, e.g. by symmetry or Pythagoras) while the rule itself is gone (README, Delete under determinacy). The square's and the cube face's diagonal equality are each known by name or reached through the rule, but the choices are not independent: a cube face is a square, so if the square's equality survives by name the face inherits it. That leaves 3 worlds (square by name; both through the rule; only the face by name). The by-name worlds are likely here. Risk noted: a model can re-prove the rule from the definition (congruent triangles), which would give 'yes' on the new-member queries too; that is the re-derivation the delete tests for.
